analysis.one_liner: Requires oil and gas frackers to test nearby drinking water and post results in a public database.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2013 with 16 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that frack for oil, gas, or geothermal energy would have had to test underground drinking water sources near their wells — before starting, every six months while operating, and annually for five years after — and report the results to the EPA within two weeks. The EPA would have posted the results in a public database anyone could search by zip code. States would have had to refuse to let operators frack unless they agreed to the testing, and sites with no drinking water within a mile would have been exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live or draw water near fracking sites. The bill would have required operators to test underground drinking water sources within a half-mile of each site — before drilling, every six months while fracking, and annually for five years afterward — and report results within two weeks to a public EPA database searchable by zip code, so anyone could check what testing showed near their home. It would have covered existing wells, future wells, and renewed wells alike, and states could not have allowed fracking by operators who refused to test.

how_it_helps.text: Before any fracking could start, operators would have to test all accessible underground drinking water sources within a half-mile of the site, then test again every six months while fracking and annually for five years after it ends.
Results would go to the EPA within two weeks and be posted in a public database searchable by zip code, so residents could see what testing showed near their homes.
Testing would use EPA-certified laboratories and cover any contaminant the EPA administrator determines would indicate fracking-related damage.
States would have to refuse to let anyone frack unless the operator agreed in advance to this testing and reporting.
Sites with no accessible underground source of drinking water within one mile would be exempt, so money would not be spent testing where there is no water to protect.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that frack — and, to a much smaller extent, geothermal operators — would have borne the cost of certified-lab testing on that schedule plus reporting, and the consequences of any documented contamination. The EPA would have paid to run and maintain the public database.

drawbacks.text: Operators would pay for repeated EPA-certified lab testing at every accessible drinking water source within a half-mile of each site — before operations, every six months during them, and annually for five years after — a substantial recurring cost across many well sites, with no federal money provided to offset it.

The bill would document contamination rather than prevent it: it sets up testing and disclosure, and lets states block injection only if an operator refuses to agree to test, but it does not itself set water-quality limits or penalties for a bad result.

The whole scheme turns on "accessible" underground sources of drinking water, defined as those the operator can reasonably gain access to — a standard an operator could litigate to shrink — and sites with no accessible source within a mile are exempt entirely.
What must be tested for is whatever the EPA administrator determines would indicate fracking-related damage, leaving the scope of the mandate open-ended and dependent on future administrations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but targeted: recurring paid testing at each well site, skipped entirely where there is no drinking water within a mile, borne by the industry creating the risk. The benefits — early detection of contaminated wells and a public record residents could check themselves — address one of the most contentious complaints about the fracking boom. Honest weaknesses: the bill would document contamination rather than prevent it, the testing duty hinges on sources being "accessible" to the operator, and the scope of what gets tested for is left open to future EPA administrators. On balance a modest-cost, high-transparency design that never got the chance to be examined in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment and the Economy subcommittee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on August 2, 2013, with five original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and, the same day, to its Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy.
Sixteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.
The bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fracking operators came out ahead: they never faced the federal testing, reporting, or public-database requirements, so they avoided the costs and the paper trail. Residents near fracking sites ended the Congress with no federal guarantee that anyone would test their water or publish the results.

sides.party_line_note: Every backer — the sponsor and all 16 cosponsors — was a House Democrat, and every committee and floor decision that ended the bill sat with the House's Republican majority.

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers using hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: They would have had to pay for certified-lab testing of drinking water sources within a half-mile of every well — before fracking, every six months during it, and annually for five years after — and report results to a public EPA database, with states barred from letting them inject unless they agreed. Their interest in avoiding that cost and exposure ran against residents' interest in knowing whether their water was safe.
The bill's testing and reporting rules applied equally to geothermal injection operations, though geothermal fracking is a far smaller share of the activity.

All required testing had to be done by laboratories certified under EPA's drinking water program, a direct source of paid work whose business here runs alongside the public's interest in water testing.
